stem_book: Passage Q.(i) to (v). The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation relates the free energy change to the enthalpy and entropy changes of the process as (ΔG)_P,T = ΔH − TΔS. The magnitude of ΔH does not change much with temperature but the entropy factor TΔS changes appreciably; thus spontaneity of a process depends very much on temperature. (i) When CaCO₃ is heated to a high temperature it decomposes into CaO and CO₂, whereas it is quite stable at room temperature. The most likely explanation is (a) ΔH overweighs TΔS at high temperature (b) TΔS overweighs ΔH at high temperature (c) at high temperature both ΔH and ΔS become negative (d) None of these. (ii) For X₂O₄(l) → 2XO₂ at 25°C, ΔH = 2.0 kcal and ΔS = 20 cal K⁻¹. The reaction would be (a) Spontaneous (b) At equilibrium (c) Unpredictable (d) Non-spontaneous. (iii) For 2A + B → C at 298 K, ΔH = 100 kcal and ΔS = 0.020 kcal K⁻¹. If ΔH and ΔS are constant over the temperature range, at what temperature will the reaction become spontaneous? (a) 1000 K (b) 3500 K (c) 5000 K (d) 1500 K. (iv) A reaction has ΔH = −20 kcal at 200 K; the reaction is spontaneous below this temperature, above it it is not. The values of ΔG and ΔS at 400 K are, respectively (a) 10, −0.1 cal K⁻¹ (b) −10 kcal, −100 cal K⁻¹ (c) 0, 10.0 cal K⁻¹ (d) 20 kcal, −100 cal K⁻¹. (v) ΔH for a certain reaction at 300 K is −15.0 kcal mol⁻¹ and ΔS is −7.2 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The free energy change and its character are (a) −12.84 kcal mol⁻¹, spontaneous (b) −12.16 kcal mol⁻¹, spontaneous (c) 12.84 kcal mol⁻¹, non-spontaneous (d) 12.0 kcal mol⁻¹, spontaneous
